note.explanation: A magnet can make a nearby piece of iron or steel act like a magnet. The end nearest the magnet gets the opposite pole, and the far end gets the other pole. When the true magnet is removed, the induced magnetism vanishes.
examples: Touch the head of an iron nail to the S-pole of a bar magnet: the nail’s near end becomes N and its far end becomes S.
Remove the bar magnet: the nail’s induced magnetism vanishes.
note.checkAnswer: The nail has induced magnetism; its near end becomes N and its far end becomes S, and the magnetism vanishes when the bar magnet is removed.
note.simple: A magnet can make an iron nail act like a magnet for a while. Take the magnet away, and the nail loses this induced magnetism.
note.checkQuestion: If the S-pole of a bar magnet touches the head of an iron nail, which pole is induced at the nail’s near end?
note.title: Induced Magnetism
steps: Place the head of an iron nail against a pole of a bar magnet.
Bring a compass near the pointed end of the nail to check that the nail acts like a magnet.
For an S-pole touching the nail, the near end becomes N and the far end becomes S.
Remove the bar magnet and check the nail again; the induced magnetism vanishes.
note.answer: The S-pole induces an N-pole at the nail’s near end and an S-pole at its far end. The induced magnetism vanishes when the true magnet is removed.

options: The nail’s near end becomes a pole opposite to the magnet’s touching pole.
The nail’s near end becomes the same pole as the magnet’s touching pole.
Both ends of the nail become north poles.
The nail cannot affect a compass.
mcqs.stem: An S-pole is brought into contact with one end of an iron nail. Which statement describes the induced poles?
rationales: This is correct because the end of the iron nearest the S-pole is induced as N.
This is wrong because the near end acquires the opposite pole, not the same pole.
This is wrong because the two ends become opposite poles, not both north poles.
This is wrong because the magnetised nail can affect a nearby compass.

options: The nail changes into a non-magnetic material.
mcqs.stem: What happens to the induced magnetism of an iron nail when the true magnet is removed?
rationales: This is wrong because the section states that induced magnetism vanishes when the true magnet is removed.
This is correct because the nail’s magnetism is induced by the nearby true magnet.
This is wrong because the nail remains iron; it does not change into another material.
This is wrong because removing the magnet from the nail does not mean the bar magnet is demagnetised.

mcqs.stem: What is it called when magnetism is produced in a magnetic material by a nearby true magnet?
rationales: This is not the best choice here because the section names the effect as induced magnetism.
This is correct because the material acquires magnetism under the influence of a true magnet.
This is wrong because demagnetization means the loss of magnetism.
This is wrong because magnetic shielding is the protection of a region from an external magnetic field.

mcqs.stem: Which material from the list can be made a magnet by induction in the activity?
rationales: This is correct because the activity uses an iron nail to demonstrate induced magnetism.
This is wrong because wood is not the magnetic material used in the activity.
This is wrong because paper is not the magnetic material used in the activity.
This is wrong because glass is not the magnetic material used in the activity.

options: The far end of the nail becomes N.
The far end of the nail becomes S.
Both ends of the nail become S.
The nail has no poles while touching the magnet.
mcqs.stem: The S-pole of a true magnet touches the head of an iron nail. What pole is induced at the far end?
rationales: This is wrong because the far end is opposite to the induced N-pole at the near end.
This is correct because the nail’s far end becomes S when the S-pole induces N at the near end.
This is wrong because the two ends of the nail become opposite poles.
This is wrong because the nail acts as a magnet while the true magnet is near it.

options: Bring a compass near the nail and observe the needle.
Heat the nail until it glows.
mcqs.stem: Which method follows the section’s activity for checking whether an iron nail has become a magnet?
rationales: This is correct because the activity checks the nail’s magnetic effect by observing a nearby compass needle.
This is wrong because heating the nail is not the test used in the activity.
This is wrong because placing the nail in water does not test its magnetic effect.
This is wrong because measuring length gives no information about magnetism.

written.text: How can you identify whether an object is a magnet or a magnetic material?
written.finalAnswer: Test the object with a known magnet. Repulsion shows that the object is a magnet; attraction alone does not prove it is a magnet, because a magnetic material can be attracted by induced magnetism.

rubric.why: Attraction alone cannot distinguish a magnet from a magnetic material.

If the object is repelled, it is a magnet.

written.text: A magnet attracts only a magnet. Explain the statement.
written.finalAnswer: The statement is not correct if taken literally. A magnet can also attract a magnetic material such as iron because it induces an opposite pole at the material’s near end. This induced magnetism vanishes when the true magnet is removed.

rubric.why: The statement needs to be clarified because magnets can attract magnetic materials too.
rubric.how: State that it is not literally true that a magnet attracts only another magnet.

rubric.why: The answer should distinguish induced magnetism from permanent magnetism.
rubric.description: State what happens after the true magnet is removed.
rubric.how: Explain that the induced magnetism vanishes when the true magnet is removed.

steps.why: The activity uses an iron nail to show that a magnetic material can become a magnet.
steps.text: Place an iron nail with its head in contact with a pole of the bar magnet.

steps.why: A compass near the nail’s far end shows whether the nail has acquired magnetism.

steps.text: The nail has become a magnet temporarily; magnetism has been induced in it.

example.question: Put a compass near to the pointed end of an iron nail. Observe the direction in which N-pole of the needle settles. Has the nail become a magnet? Has magnetism been induced in it?
example.answer: Yes. The iron nail has become a magnet temporarily, so magnetism has been induced in it.

explain.title: A magnetic material can be made a magnet
explain.body: Your textbook states: “Magnetic material such as iron or steel can be made a magnet. This is known as magnetization.” In other words, magnetism has been induced in the material.

explain.title: The ends get opposite poles
explain.body: Your textbook states: “From the above activity, we conclude that the S-pole of the true magnet induces N-pole in the near end of the piece of iron (nail) while the far end of the iron piece becomes S-pole as shown in the figure.”

explain.title: The induced magnetism vanishes
explain.body: Your textbook states: “It should be noted that the induced magnetism vanishes as the true magnet is removed.” So the nail does not keep this induced magnetism after the magnet is taken away.

explain.title: Use a compass to observe the effect
explain.body: A compass needle responds to the magnetic effect of the nail. Check the needle near the nail while the bar magnet is touching it, then check again after removing the bar magnet.

mistakes: Do not say that the near end gets the same pole as the pole touching it; it gets the opposite pole.
Do not say that the induced magnetism remains after the true magnet is removed; it vanishes.
Do not use attraction alone as proof that an object is a magnet; a magnetic material can also be attracted.
When describing the nail, state the poles at both ends, not only the pole at the end near the magnet.
